description: We are Opportunity Mission, passionate about space exploration and planetary cartography. Inspired by the legacy of the Opportunity rover, we are building an interactive Mars map. We have experience in web development, 3D visualization, and spatial data analysis. We are looking for curious minds in UX/UI design, programming, data science, or space storytelling. Join us and let's keep exploring the Red Planet together!
summary:
Oppy Trail: Making Mars Navigable

Opportunity Mission developed Oppy Trail, an offline planetary exploration and navigation platform that transforms real NASA and USGS datasets into interactive maps, 3D terrain visualizations, and terrain-aware route planning. Designed as a “Google Maps for Mars,” it allows users to explore four real Martian regions, identify potential hazards, and evaluate routes based on slope constraints, obstacles, estimated travel time, radiation exposure, and a 7-hour EVA window.
By turning complex scientific and geospatial information into accessible, actionable insights, Oppy Trail addresses the challenge of making planetary exploration data easier to understand and use. Its integrated tools support scientific education, public outreach, and analog mission planning, without requiring internet access or specialized GIS software.
Our next steps include expanding Martian coverage, integrating mission telemetry and interactive climate layers, and developing collaborative analysis and intelligent terrain-assistance tools with human validation and traceable data.
Our vision is to make learning about Mars as straightforward as opening a map. Oppy Trail is the first step: a map that does not invent the planet, but makes it navigable.
details:
1. CONCEPT

What Oppy Trail Does?

The Opportunity Mission team presents Oppy Trail, an offline planetary navigation platform that transforms real Martian geospatial and scientific data into an interactive environment for terrain exploration, route planning, and operational decision-making.

Inspired by the familiarity of Google Maps, the platform brings together multiple datasets from NASA, JPL, and the USGS to help users understand the Martian surface not just as a landscape, but as terrain that must be carefully assessed before traversing it.

Explore, Analyze, and Navigate

The platform allows users to explore four real regions of Mars, examine terrain elevation and environmental conditions, calculate routes that avoid steep slopes, rocks, and sand dunes, and experience a journey from a rover's first-person perspective. The entire application operates offline and requires no user account.

At the core of Oppy Trail is a route planner designed to account for the challenges of navigating the Martian surface.

Rather than simply finding the shortest path, the system evaluates terrain conditions and identifies routes that avoid steep slopes, sand dunes, rocks, and restricted areas.

Each route provides key operational information, including distance, estimated travel time, radiation exposure estimates, and whether the journey fits within a 7-hour Extravehicular Activity (EVA) window.

Users can move seamlessly between global and detailed views, examine terrain elevation and geological features, identify potential hazards, and visualize the surface in both 2D and 3D.

The platform also includes the Oppy assistant, an interactive guided tour, and an exportable mission log that allows users to document their exploration.

Oppy Trail transforms real Martian scientific data into actionable exploration decisions, making planetary navigation more accessible, understandable, and safer.

What the Current Version Includes

  • Four real Martian regions: Two within Jezero Crater (Perseverance mission) and two within Gale Crater (Curiosity mission).
  • 60.52 km² of mapped terrain: Using high-resolution imagery and a digital elevation model.
  • 23,730 automatically detected rocks: Identified across Jezero imagery, including rocks measuring 1.5 meters or larger.
  • 11,429 map tiles: Enabling seamless navigation from a global view of Mars down to detailed terrain exploration.
  • Terrain-aware route planning: Avoiding slopes steeper than 20° or 25°, sand dunes, and restricted areas.
  • Intuitive terrain risk assessment: A color-coded classification system, green (safe), amber (caution), and red (prohibited).
  • 3D terrain visualization: Alongside a first-person rover simulation with operational telemetry.
  • The complete application runs offline, requires no account creation or external servers, and is distributed as a lightweight 176 MB package that can be launched locally or accessed through a web link.

2. IMPACT

Scientific Education, Public Outreach, and Open Access

Oppy Trail addresses a fundamental challenge in planetary exploration: scientific data is abundant, but transforming it into information that people can understand and use for decision-making remains difficult. Terrain elevation, slope gradients, craters, rocks, radiation, and operational constraints become tangible elements that users can explore and understand.

Our goal is to bridge that gap by making real Martian terrain data accessible not only to researchers and engineers, but also to students, educators, space enthusiasts, and future explorers. Safe and informed mobility is essential for the success of future robotic and human missions to Mars. Slopes, rocks, dunes, radiation exposure, and operational time constraints can all influence where and how an exploration mission can proceed.

Oppy Trail brings these considerations together in a single environment, helping users compare routes, identify potential hazards, and understand the operational implications of traversing different areas. The platform also promotes space science outreach by transforming satellite imagery and planetary measurements into an engaging experience for people without a background in geospatial sciences.

Although the current platform is an exploratory and planning tool rather than a certified flight-navigation system, its approach demonstrates how publicly available planetary datasets can be transformed into practical mission-planning resources. The Oppy assistant, guided tour, and child-friendly version make it possible to communicate the same scientific content to audiences of different ages and backgrounds, without compromising the underlying data.

Its offline functionality reduces dependence on internet connectivity and makes planetary exploration and mission planning more accessible to analog missions, universities, schools, and science exhibitions.

Looking ahead, the team aims to expand open access to planetary cartographic knowledge by incorporating additional Martian regions while maintaining full data traceability: identifying the source file behind each dataset, its spatial resolution, and its intended application.

Our impact goes beyond making Mars easier to visualize. We want to make the knowledge needed to explore it easier to access, understand, and use.

3. CREATIVITY AND INNOVATION

What if exploring Mars could be as intuitive as navigating a city on Earth?

This question inspired Oppy Trail.

While planetary missions generate enormous amounts of scientific and geospatial information, accessing and interpreting that information often requires specialized tools and technical expertise. We wanted to create a different experience: an integrated platform where complex Martian data becomes something people can explore, interpret, and use to make decisions.

A Tribute to Opportunity, Building around a Legacy of Exploration

The project's name comes from NASA's Opportunity rover, affectionately known as Oppy, which far exceeded its originally planned mission lifetime. Designed to operate for just 90 Martian days, Opportunity explored the Red Planet for nearly 15 years and traveled more than 45 kilometers.

In June 2018, the rover lost communication with Earth after an intense dust storm enveloped its location, preventing its solar panels from receiving sufficient sunlight. NASA officially declared the mission complete on February 13, 2019.

We chose this name because we wanted our project to reflect the same spirit of exploration: going beyond what is expected and finding new ways to understand the Red Planet.Opportunity's story represents perseverance, discovery, and the extraordinary possibilities of engineering.

Our innovation is not simply about displaying an image of Mars. It is about transforming vast amounts of scientific information into meaningful, accessible, and actionable decisions. Through Opportunity Mission, we aim to ensure that Oppy's legacy continues to inspire exploration while providing something useful to everyone who opens the application.

What Makes Oppy Trail Different

  • An integrated exploration environment: Maps, terrain risk assessment, route planning, radiation exposure, 3D visualization, and first-person simulation are combined into a single application.
  • Risk communicated through meaningful data: Hazards are explained through an intuitive visual classification system supported by measurable values, rather than decorative colors alone.
  • Fully offline operation: No internet connection, user accounts, or external servers are required, making the platform suitable for fieldwork, classrooms, and science exhibitions.
  • An interactive mission experience: Users become active participants through mission logs, a black box recording system, and the Oppy assistant.

4. Data Processing and Integration

a. Data Acquisition All inputs are public and require no API keys: HiRISE and CTX orthoimagery distributed through NASA Mars Trek, digital elevation models from USGS (MOLA/HRSC-derived), CRISM mineral maps for Jezero, MEDA weather records from Perseverance, RAD/Curiosity radiation data, and the official NASA landing-site coordinates. Four regions are processed in detail: two in Jezero crater and two in Gale crater, covering 60.52 km².

b. Spatial Mapping & Rendering The DEM is reprojected onto a geographic grid aligned with Mars Trek, using the Martian radius (3,396,190 m) so distances and slopes are true to Mars rather than inherited from Earth. Cells are 10 m; slope (p90), roughness, dunes and sand ripples are computed per cell and combined into a risk value from 0 to 1. The result is served as a tile pyramid from zoom 9 to 17 (11,429 tiles), plus 3D relief meshes and a binary planning grid used by the A* planner.

c. Interactive Overlays Dynamic layers can be switched on top of the base map: risk, slope, forbidden zones at 20° and 25°, dark dunes, sand ripples, rock density and CRISM minerals in Jezero, each with opacity control. Routes are drawn as GeoJSON overlays with start/goal markers, and the app adds the six historic NASA landing sites, points of interest, and rock detections from BoulderNet (23,730 rocks ≥ 1.5 m). Clicking the terrain opens an inspector with elevation, slope, risk and rock count for that exact cell.

5. Tools and Architecture

Frontend / UI HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript (ES modules) — no framework and no build step, so the whole app runs from a folder with double-click or from any static host. The interface is responsive, keyboard-driven and fully bilingual-ready, with a guided tour and an offline assistant (Oppy) built on rule-based intents.

Mapping & Visualization

  • Leaflet for the 2D map, tile pyramid and layer control.
  • Three.js + OrbitControls for the 3D terrain viewer and the first-person POV simulation.
  • Custom JavaScript for the A* planner (8 neighbors), the risk-cost model, the elevation profile (canvas) and the tile/grid loaders.
  • The stack is 100% client-side: there is no backend, database or external service at runtime; all data ships with the site (176 MB, fully offline).

Data Formats

  • GeoJSON for routes, forbidden zones, rock detections and points of interest.
  • JSON for the region manifest, per-region metadata (layers, bounds, centroids), mission panel and weather data.
  • Binary grid + JSON metadata (grid.bin / grid.json) for the 10 m planning mesh consumed by A*.
  • Raster tiles (PNG/JPEG, z9–z17) for the map and analysis layers; GeoTIFF as the original source format.
  • GPX for route export and CSV for the mission black-box log.

Development Methodology

The development process was structured into five key phases:

  • Planning: Defining project objectives, tasks, responsibilities, and expected deliverables.
  • Research: Collecting satellite imagery, geospatial datasets, and scientific reference sources.
  • Development: Processing information, analyzing Martian terrain, and building the platform's individual modules.
  • Integration and Testing: Connecting the different components and evaluating the overall system's functionality and performance.
  • Presentation: Documenting results, preparing the user guide, and developing the final project demonstration.

Version Control and Deliverables

The project is organized around versioned data packages and website releases. Each region documents its original source files, spatial resolution, and associated data layers. Every release is identified by a version number and accompanied by a manifest that enables reproducibility.

This approach ensures that any result or feature reviewed by the judges can be traced back to its original source data, providing transparency, consistency, and scientific accountability throughout the project.

Digital Tools and Development Resources

The development of Oppy Trail involved a combination of scientific platforms and digital tools, including NASA Mars Exploration resources, Mars Trek, USGS, JMARS, and Google Earth Pro for planetary data research, terrain analysis, and geospatial visualization. Python supported data processing and application development, while additional digital tools facilitated documentation, data organization, and project coordination.

6. FUTURE GOALS

The next step is to establish Oppy Trail as a comprehensive Martian exploration platform serving education, public outreach, and analog missions. The team's future objectives include:

  • Expanding Martian coverage by incorporating new regions using the same standardized data-processing workflow.
  • Integrating active mission telemetry and interactive climate data layers.
  • Developing traversal simulations and collaborative tools for scientific analysis.
  • Exploring intelligent assistance features to support terrain interpretation, always backed by human validation and traceable data sources.
  • Bridging virtual exploration with educational experiences and scientific research.
  • Exploring applications in scientific and astronomical tourism through virtual tours and interactive experiences that bring Martian exploration closer to the public.

Opportunity Mission envisions a future where learning about Mars is as straightforward as opening a map. Oppy Trail is the first step: a map that does not invent the planet, but makes it navigable.

7. TEAM WORKFLOW

A Team of Six Complementary Skill Sets

Opportunity Mission is composed of six members with backgrounds in engineering, technology, research, tourism, architecture, and sustainability. This diversity allowed us to assign responsibilities according to each member's strengths and bring together different perspectives throughout the development of the project, including technical, scientific, spatial, and communication-focused approaches.

EVIDENCE OF WORK

Opportunity Mission — Official Platform Demo

Explore Our Platform: Full System Walkthrough

Here is a brief tour of our platform, starting with a Quick Start Guide where you can register your name, define your mission, and review the scientific data inputs powering the system. You can switch between different specialized map layers, such as mineral composition and hazard/risk maps, and interact with OPPY, our built-in AI chatbot, to ask technical questions in real time.

Next, we demonstrate how to plot a path using our smart route planner, allowing you to choose between an on-foot traverse or a rover route. During navigation, you have access to live telemetry data, an emergency button in case of an incident, and multiple camera perspectives, including a first-person (POV) view, a rear third-person view, and an interactive 3D map mode with playback speed controls. Finally, the platform covers four distinct regions and lets you simulate and explore how environmental conditions behave across every hour of the day.

Thank You for Exploring Opportunity Mission! 🚀 Long Live Oppy! 🛰️✨
